name: Baré
confidence_why: Oliveira 1993 and Aikhenvald 1995, the only two first-hand descriptions and both drawn from the same last fluent speaker, agree that stress falls on the penult in two- and three-syllable words and on the antepenult in longer suffixed words, but Aikhenvald 1995 presents this as contrastive stress with frequency tendencies and a three-syllable window rather than a fixed rule (both cite the minimal pair kurí 'surubim' / kúri 'spring'), so the predictable-stress coding is the better reading rather than a settled one.

(1) /ku`ri/ "surubim" /`kuri/ "ijapó". Por outro lado, em grande parte das palavras da língua a posição do acento é predizível por uma regra geral; há exceções que podem ser explicadas por regras específicas de acordo com a propriedade acentual de cada formativo da palavra. ... a) Regra geral: Em palavras de duas e três sílabas o acento recai sobre a penúltima; em palavras de quatro ou mais sílabas o acento recai sobre a antepenúltima; Dessa maneira, a maioria das palavras é paroxítona ou proparoxítona. tone_statements.citation: Aikhenvald, Alexandra Y. 1999. Areal diffusion and language contact in the Içana-Vaupés basin, north-west Amazonia. In R. M. W. Dixon & Alexandra Y. Aikhenvald (eds.), The Amazonian Languages (Cambridge Language Surveys), 385-416. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
tone_statements.quote: 4.1 Pitch accent. Pitch accent (a low-high distinction) is a property of all the languages spoken in the Vaupés. It is also found in Baniwa and Kurripako (e.g. Valadares 1994), but is absent from Warekena and Bare, North Arawak languages spoken outside the area (Aikhenvald 1995a, 1998). [Table 14.2 'Properties shared by languages of the Içana-Vaupés': pitch accent -- East Tucano: yes; Tariana: yes; Dâw, Hupda: yes; Baniwa: yes; Warekena, Bare (North Arawak languages outside this area): no]
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: No tone and no pitch accent in Bare (explicitly contrasted with the low-high pitch accent of Baniwa/Tariana/East Tucano); word prosody = contrastive stress.

audit.recode_to: 'descriptions disagree' between Oliveira 1993:55-58 (count-based general rule: 2-3σ penult, 4+σ antepenult, with morpheme-specific overrides) and Aikhenvald 1995:9-10 (contrastive stress; placement 'depends on the accentual properties of morphemes'; prefixes extraprosodic, suffixes accented vs extraprosodic; polysyllables only bounded by an antepenult window; final nasal vowels always stressed) — or, if one class must be chosen, the catalog's lexical/morphological-accent class with a right-edge three-syllable window and penult default (StressTyp2-style P;LEX) rather than pure count-dependent 'fixed'. Either way: add Aikhenvald 1995:9 as co-source, delete the 'different last speaker' conjecture (same consultant, Candelário da Silva, 1991), and note that StressTyp2's paraphrase 'longer words have penultimate stress with antepenultimate exceptions' over-reads p.9 (that sentence is about trisyllables; for polysyllables Aikhenvald states only the antepenult window).
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Oliveira 1993 scan we hold at §3.1 pp.55-58 (page scan viewed; scanned q63-q66) and §1.6 p.21 (scanned q29). sources.citation: Aikhenvald, Alexandra Y. 1995. Bare. (Languages of the World/Materials 100.) München/Newcastle: Lincom Europa. 57 pp. [open copy uploaded to the Internet Archive by the author (uploader a.y.aikhenvald@live.com), item 'the-amazonian-languages.-copy.-cambridge-language-surveys', file ]
sources.quote: p.9: 'Bare has contrastive stress, e.g. the following minimal pair: kuɻí "surubim: a kind of fish" and kúɻi "a spring". In disyllabic monomorphemic words, the stress falls most frequently on the first syllable, e.g. mába "bee", dápa "pacca". Occasionally, the last syllable is stressed, e.g. beké "future marker". In trisyllabic words the stress falls most frequently on the penultimate syllable, e.g. mukáwa "rifle", yawáke "yesterday", more rarely it falls on the antepenultimate syllable, e.g. i-d'ékada "he made". sources.note: §4.1 states that pitch accent (a low-high distinction), areal in the Vaupés and present in Baniwa/Kurripako, is ABSENT from Warekena and Bare; Table 14.2 row 'pitch accent' codes 'Warekena, Bare' = no (vs yes for East Tucano, Tariana, Dâw/Hupda, Baniwa). No lexical tone is attributed to Bare anywhere in the volume (ch.3 p.79 lists Bare among contrastive-stress languages and not among the family's tone or pitch accent languages).
